project_tracker_diagnostic: Strongly branched plant with a broomy look; many small yellow heads; narrow leaves; whole-plant architecture is one of the best identification characters.

project_inclusion.learning_reason: Common and useful Central Texas field-learning taxon.

morphology_keys.leaves: Alternate, narrow, linear to oblanceolate, often becoming reduced upward.
morphology_keys.heads: Many tiny yellow RADIATE heads with separate ray florets and central disc florets, usually in crowded corymbiform flat-to-rounded arrays on terminal branches. Do not call discoid: Flora of North America and UT Austin describe rays + discs.
morphology_keys.phyllaries: 12–15 involucral phyllaries with pale/whitish resinous faces, 1-veined without a narrow GREEN BORDER along the dorsal nerve (unlike sometimes-green-nerved Gutierrezia texana). Need a true macro to teach this.
morphology_keys.fruit: Cypselae with a pappus of scales.
best_field_traits: Yellow RAY and DISC florets, not discoid
Disc pappus has long basally united scales (verify under hand lens)

photo_strategy.selection_logic: Prefer curated taxon photos plus multiple views from one Central Texas/Texas observation.

look_here_first: Find many small YELLOW RADIATE heads crowded in roughly level or rounded terminal clusters. Confirm with pale whitish phyllaries lacking green nerve borders and longer DISC-floret pappus scales; compare Gutierrezia texana and Amphiachyris amoena before naming.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Amphiachyris dracunculoides tends toward crowded corymb-like arrays; A. amoena has open paniculate arrays. Both are radiate. In comparison with Gutierrezia texana, the disc pappus scales are long (almost disc-corolla length) versus very short or nearly absent, while Amphiachyris phyllary nerves lack narrow green borders.
